The survey is described as a household survey with a sample drawn to be representative of the target population of 16-to-65-year-olds in the Slovak Republic, and analyses are stated to check for non-response bias. The note does not specify the exact sampling weight variable name(s) or any replicate-weight scheme (e.g., BRR/jackknife), so the precise weighting mechanics cannot be extracted from the provided text. For analysts using the underlying Survey of Adult Skills microdata, complex survey weights should be applied as recommended in the Survey’s Reader’s Companion/technical documentation to account for unequal selection probabilities and clustering; doorstep respondents are generally excluded when comparing across cycles to maintain comparability.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: The Slovak Republic participated in the Survey of Adult Skills 2022-23. The analytic sample described in the note is the set of 5,238 adults who participated in the survey (overall response rate 70%), drawn to be representative of about 3.6 million 16-to-65-year-olds residing in the country. The note indicates that doorstep respondents (administered only the doorstep questionnaire due to language barriers) are generally excluded when comparing results across cycles (2011-12 vs 2022-23) to maximize comparability; the figures/notes explicitly state this exclusion for cycle-comparison results.

data.outcome_summary: The OECD Survey of Adult Skills 2023 country note for the Slovak Republic summarizes adult proficiency in three domains—literacy, numeracy, and adaptive problem solving—assessed in 2022-23 among adults aged 16-65. The assessment is administered exclusively on digital tablets and proficiency is reported on 500-point scales with proficiency levels (e.g., Level 1 or below; Levels 4–5). In the Slovak Republic, mean performance is 254 in literacy, 261 in numeracy, and 247 in adaptive problem solving, with 24% at Level 1 or below in literacy and 3% at Levels 4–5; similar level distributions are reported for numeracy and adaptive problem solving. The note also reports how skills relate to outcomes: higher numeracy is associated with better labour-force participation (a one-standard-deviation increase in numeracy corresponds to a 2-percentage-point higher likelihood), and high proficiency is linked to higher life satisfaction and health. For cross-cycle comparisons, doorstep respondents are excluded to improve comparability, and uncertainty is communicated via 95% confidence intervals around mean estimates.
